title: I’m Part of the Team Writing the Next Bible of Psychiatry—For the First Time, the DSM Will Use Biology to Understand Mental Disorders - Nautilus
gist: A DSM strategic-committee member explains that the next edition of psychiatry's diagnostic manual will, for the first time, begin integrating neurobiology—cautiously, because valid biomarkers for mental illness still barely exist and environment heavily shapes these brain disorders.

insights.claim: The American Psychiatric Association plans to release the next DSM in the coming years and, for the first time, integrate biology into psychiatric diagnosis.
insights.speaker: Anand Kumar
insights.so_what: A structural shift in how mental illness is diagnosed that could reshape diagnostics, drug trials, and mental-health markets.
insights.locator: one of its major plans is to modernize the manual by introducing biology

insights.claim: The DSM has never previously incorporated biology into its diagnoses because the underlying biology of mental illness was considered too preliminary for such a widely used clinical manual.
insights.speaker: Anand Kumar
insights.so_what: Explains the historical gap the new edition is trying to close and why it stayed open so long.
insights.locator: the DSM has never integrated biology in its diagnoses

insights.claim: The DSM-5 (2013) drew criticism that its lack of objective biological measures risks medicalizing human suffering and reducing the validity of psychiatric diagnoses.
insights.speaker: Anand Kumar
insights.so_what: Frames the credibility problem driving reform of the manual.
insights.locator: attracted significant criticism from clinicians and researchers

insights.claim: The author served on the DSM strategic committee from May 2024 to August 2026 and worked on the subcommittee tasked with integrating neurobiology, and says the team is taking a deliberately nuanced approach.
insights.speaker: Anand Kumar
insights.so_what: Signals the reform is incremental, not a wholesale switch to biology-based diagnosis.
insights.locator: I was a member of the DSM’s strategic committee

insights.claim: There are currently no scientifically valid biomarkers for any psychiatric condition, with the exception of certain proteins used to diagnose Alzheimer's disease.
insights.speaker: Anand Kumar
insights.so_what: Sets a hard baseline: any diagnostic-biomarker claims in mental health should be treated skeptically today.
insights.quote: There are currently no scientifically valid biomarkers for any psychiatric condition, with the exception of certain proteins used to diagnose Alzheimer’s disease.
insights.locator: Why Aren’t There Biomarkers for Mental Illness?

insights.claim: Biomarkers are routine elsewhere in medicine—hemoglobin A1C for diabetes, cholesterol for cardiovascular risk, CT scans for tumor size—highlighting how far psychiatry lags the rest of medicine.
insights.speaker: Anand Kumar
insights.so_what: Benchmarks the diagnostic gap psychiatry must close to reach precision-medicine standards.
insights.locator: Biomarkers are widely used in medicine.

insights.claim: Serious mental illnesses are brain disorders with large psychological and social components, and strong environmental influences like trauma and family history make it hard to isolate biological from psychosocial causes.
insights.speaker: Anand Kumar
insights.so_what: Explains why a clean, lab-measurable signal for mental illness is intrinsically difficult to find.
insights.locator: These strong environmental influences make it challenging

insights.claim: Psychiatric disorders are conceptualized as overlapping behavioral syndromes rather than discrete illnesses, so a single biomarker reflecting multiple processes at once is unrealistic.
insights.speaker: Anand Kumar
insights.so_what: Argues against expecting one-test-per-disorder diagnostics; subtyping is the more likely path.
insights.locator: researchers conceptualize psychiatric disorders not as discrete illnesses but behavioral syndromes

insights.claim: Conditions like major depressive disorder and schizophrenia likely contain several subgroups that look similar but arise through different mechanisms and pathways.
insights.speaker: Anand Kumar
insights.so_what: Implies future diagnosis and drug targeting will fragment single diagnoses into biologically distinct subtypes.
insights.locator: likely have several subgroups that superficially resemble each other

insights.claim: In March 2025 the FDA approved a blood test detecting specific amyloid and tau protein forms to help confirm Alzheimer's, the first biomarker for a disorder affecting both brain and behavior.
insights.speaker: Anand Kumar
insights.so_what: A proof-of-concept that brain-and-behavior disorders can get validated blood biomarkers—watch for diagnostics adoption.
insights.locator: In March 2025, the Food and Drug Administration approved a blood test

insights.claim: About 30% of patients with depression have high C-reactive protein levels, suggesting CRP could flag a depression subtype that responds better to certain treatments.
insights.speaker: Anand Kumar
insights.so_what: An inflammation-based biomarker could enable treatment stratification in depression care.
insights.locator: Approximately 30% of patients with depression have high CRP levels

insights.claim: Bundling individual genetic risk variants—whose effects are cumulative—into a polygenic risk score could give a more comprehensive estimate of mental-disorder risk, though it is not yet clinic-ready.
insights.speaker: Anand Kumar
insights.so_what: Genetic risk scoring is a leading-but-immature path toward precision psychiatry to monitor.
insights.locator: Bundling these individual genetic variants into what’s called a polygenic risk score

insights.claim: In a 2013 survey, 65% of clinician respondents predicted the DSM-6 would include laboratory tests to diagnose psychiatric disorders.
insights.speaker: Anand Kumar
insights.so_what: Shows long-standing professional expectation for lab-based psychiatric diagnosis, now partly materializing.
insights.locator: 65% of respondents predicted the DSM-6 will include laboratory tests

insights.claim: The author's stated vision is that patients could one day arrive at the clinic with genetic tests, brain scans, and blood work enabling more precise diagnoses and personalized psychiatric treatment.
insights.speaker: Anand Kumar
insights.so_what: Maps the long-run direction of travel for mental-health diagnostics and personalized care.
insights.locator: One day, patients may be able to walk into the clinic
